greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace be with you all as we gather in the presence of our loving God.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you are the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Lord, have mercy.
Christ Jesus, you raise us from death to new and eternal life. Christ, have mercy.
Lord Jesus, you fill our hearts with joy when your glory appears. Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: Lord, when your glory appears, my joy will be full.
homily:
We often talk about hope as if it were a delicate thing—a fragile little bird kept in a warm room, something that a sudden draft could blow out. We treat hope like a wish we make when we blow out candles on a birthday cake, or a polite optimism we put on when we walk out the front door so the neighbors won't worry. But Saint Paul, writing to the Corinthians today, is not talking about polite optimism. He is talking about the foundation of the world. He looks us straight in the eye and tells us something stark and unyielding: "If for this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are the most pitiable people of all." 

Think about the weight of those words. Paul isn't smoothing over the edges of our grief. He isn't offering us cheap comfort or a cheerful platitude to hang on the wall. He is naming the exact terror that sits quietly in the chest of anyone who has ever loved deeply and then stood by an open grave. He is saying: if this world—this broken, fleeting, fragile world of goodbyes and empty chairs—is all there is, then our love is a tragedy. If death has the final word, then every tear we shed, every early morning ache, every memory we hold onto like a lifeline is nothing more than a cruel joke. Paul goes right down into the dark room where we keep our most painful questions, and he turns the light on. He doesn't pretend the room is empty. He looks at the very worst thing—the finality of the tomb, the silence of the grave, the cold reality of human mortality—and he refuses to let it win. 

Because right after he lays out that terrifying thought, he shatters it with a sentence that changes the architecture of human history: "But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep."

There it is. The hinge of the universe. The firstfruits.

I want you to think about that image for a moment—the firstfruits. In the ancient world, the farmer didn't wait until the entire harvest was safely gathered into the barn before he offered thanks to God. Before the bins were full, before the work was done, before the long winter set in, he took the very first green shoot, the very first ripening cluster from the vine, and he brought it to the altar. Why? Because that first fruit was the guarantee of everything that was to come. It was the proof that the earth was alive, that the seed planted in the dark had not died in vain, that the sun was faithful. When Paul calls Christ the "firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," he is telling us that the resurrection of Jesus is not an isolated miracle that happened two thousand years ago to one extraordinary man. It is the prototype. It is the first green shoot bursting through the hard, frozen earth of our despair. It means the whole harvest belongs to God. Every single soul we have loved and handed back to the Maker is part of that same harvest.

And when we think about this, my friends, we are drawn straight to the memory of our dear Benjamin. 

Benjamin Vo was a boy who understood how things were built. He had that brilliant, sharp mind—a true photocopy of his father, looking at the world with a tireless, beautiful curiosity. Whether he was diving into GitHub repositories, exploring cloud infrastructure, or dreaming up the cheerful ambition of 'con chim airlines'—a project he would talk about with that irresistible, bubbling giggle—Ben loved systems that connected. He loved seeing how the pieces fit together. But beneath the logic, beneath the mathematics, beneath the bright ambition of a fifteen-year-old boy who saw the world as a vast, exciting map to be explored, there was a gentle soul. 

Think of the sweetness of him. Think of a boy who, unprompted, wanted to hand over his entire piggy bank to help his uncle who was struggling with his health. He didn't break it open. He didn't make a show of it. He didn't demand a headline. He simply offered. That is what a firstfruit looks like. That is a heart already tuned to the frequency of heaven. 

Alan and Thao, I know the silence in your home. I know that these past three months have felt like a winter that refuses to end. You look around at the spaces he filled—the laughter, the aviation talk, the morning greetings—and the world feels thin, almost transparent with absence. You remember the dreams, like the one where Dad walked with him and Ben paid for the ice cream, or that vivid night when Ben stood outside a hospital room door in his green shorts, looking strong and tall, trying to make sense of a world that didn't make sense, before turning with that tender, mếu máo face to say, "Không sao đâu, con sẽ dõi theo ba mẹ"—it's okay, I will watch over mom and dad. 

Listen to those words today. Let them land in the quiet places of your heart. Ben is not lost to the cold winds of this earth. He is gathered into the firstfruits. He is standing in the light of the One who conquered the grave. 

And Ryan, my dear brother, I know how much you miss your partner in adventure, your brother who shared the roller coasters, the laughter, and the journey. You carry his name and his spirit in your own heartbeat. When you feel quiet, remember that the bond between brothers is forged in eternity. He is cheering for you, walking beside you in the unseen places, whispering to keep dreaming and keep living with that same bright, generous heart.

Sometimes, in the quiet of grief, a heavy, silent stone settles into the hearts of parents and loved ones. You find yourselves replaying the past, wondering if there was something missed, whispering that terrible, unanswerable question to the dark. If that stone is resting on your chest today, hear the Gospel answer it. When the disciples asked Jesus who sinned that a man was born blind, Jesus didn't assign blame; He said, "Neither this man nor his parents." Illness and sorrow are never a punishment, and they are never the fault of those who loved and cared with every ounce of their strength. You missed nothing. You are not to blame. God does not accuse you, and you must not accuse yourselves. Let that stone fall today. Be as gentle with your own hearts as Benjamin was with everyone around him. 

Look at the Psalm we prayed today: "Hide me in the shadow of your wings... on waking, I shall be content in your presence." That is where Ben is. He is resting beneath the shadow of those wings. His brilliant mind, his gentle smile, his aviation dreams, his deep love for his family—none of that was wasted. God does not create a masterpiece only to shatter it into nothingness. He gathers every single piece. 

So what do you carry out these doors today? It is something very small, but very real. The next time the grief catches you unawares—when the house is too quiet or a memory flashes across your mind—do not try to push it away. Take a breath. Whisper his name, and then whisper the name of Jesus. Remember that you are a family held together by a love that death cannot touch. Keep walking. Keep loving. Keep trusting. The harvest has begun, and the firstfruits are safe in the hands of God. Amen.
standing_petitions: For Benjamin and all who have fallen asleep in Christ, that they now rest in the eternal light and joy of His presence.
For all who grieve the loss of a child or loved one, that God console their hearts and fill them with the unshakable hope of the resurrection.
communion: My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may His resurrection be the light that guides your steps today and always. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
Brothers and sisters:
If Christ is preached as raised from the dead,
how can some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead?
If there is no resurrection of the dead,
then neither has Christ been raised.
And if Christ has not been raised, then empty too is our preaching;
empty, too, your faith.
Then we are also false witnesses to God,
because we testified against God that he raised Christ,
whom he did not raise if in fact the dead are not raised.
For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised,
and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain;
you are still in your sins.
Then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
If for this life only we have hoped in Christ,
we are the most pitiable people of all.But now Christ has been raised from the dead,
the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (15b) Lord, when your glory appears, my joy will be full.
Hear, O LORD, a just suit;
attend to my outcry;
hearken to my prayer from lips without deceit. 
R. Lord, when your glory appears, my joy will be full.
I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; 
incline your ear to me; hear my word.
Show your wondrous mercies,
O savior of those who flee 
from their foes to refuge at your right hand.
R. Lord, when your glory appears, my joy will be full.
Hide me in the shadow of your wings,
But I in justice shall behold your face;
on waking, I shall be content in your presence.
R. Lord, when your glory appears, my joy will be full.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
Jesus journeyed from one town and village to another,
preaching and proclaiming the good news of the Kingdom of God.
Accompanying him were the Twelve
and some women who had been cured of evil spirits and infirmities,
Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
Joanna, the wife of Herod’s steward Chuza,
Susanna, and many others
who provided for them out of their resources.

pet_prayers.text: What happened my son? It's been 3 months since you left us. Missing you so much my whole body aches. Mom cries every day now... What are we going to do now Ben?  Please pray for us.

pet_prayers.text:
Hey Ben,

Rafael Rizzo and his little brother Ben really need your help right now. Please bless them with good health and give them the strength to get through this together. Please watch over Brandon and Flor's health, too.

I miss you a whole bunch. I know you're up in heaven watching over all of us. Whenever you're able to, stop by to visit, yeah? I love you and miss you so much!

Please pray for me and mom to have good health and strength.
